# AI Coding Assistants

The RZMPS skill helps coding assistants create and debug Three.js particle systems and VFX,
compose emitters, modules, spatial effects, and renderers, and validate WebGL and WebGPU
output using actual canvas previews. The complete skill lives in the public GitHub repository
at [.agents/skills/rzmps](https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps/tree/HEAD/.agents/skills/rzmps).
Its entry point and references are generated from these canonical human guides and API declarations.

## Installation

Choose an installation explicitly after reviewing the skill and authorizing any changes to
agent configuration. Installing `@rzmps/rzmps` with npm never installs a skill automatically.

<!-- distribution:installation:start -->
```bash
# Discover available skills
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --list

# Install the RZMPS skill
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --skill rzmps

# Install globally (optional)
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --skill rzmps -g
```
<!-- distribution:installation:end -->

The CLI lets you select compatible agents. Project installation affects the current project;
`-g` installs at user scope. The skill follows the [Agent Skills format](https://agentskills.io/specification).
Compatible installers discover it directly from GitHub; no manual registry submission is required.
See the [skills CLI documentation](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) for agent selection and installation options.

These shorthand commands read the repository's default branch. They become available once
this skill is committed and published there. Before that, test the actual checkout with
`npx skills add . --list`, or use a published branch URL such as
`https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps/tree/develop` in place of `rzmay/rzmps`.
Local validation does not prove that unpushed files are already discoverable from GitHub.

## Lightweight npm Guidance

<!-- distribution:npm-readme:start -->
The optional [RZMPS skill](https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps/tree/HEAD/.agents/skills/rzmps)
helps coding assistants build Three.js particle systems and VFX using emitters, modules,
renderers, and WebGL/WebGPU previews.

```bash
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --skill rzmps
```

Review the skill and authorize installation before changing agent configuration.
The npm package includes a short generated `AGENTS.md`, without bundling the full skill or
its references. These entry points do not guarantee automatic agent discovery. For the
installed version's API, inspect `build/index.d.ts` and the package version; see the
[canonical documentation](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/) for guides.
<!-- distribution:npm-readme:end -->

## Discovery and Maintenance

The repository, this documentation site, the npm README, and generated `llms.txt` all point
to the same canonical skill in GitHub. `llms.txt` includes explicit installation guidance;
the website does not host another copy of the skill or its bundled references.

`llms-full.txt` is an optional generated Markdown bundle of the guides, examples, and API
reference for tools that need a complete documentation snapshot. It is a convenience format,
not a requirement for skill discovery, installation, or automatic agent access. Prefer the
index and relevant pages when the full bundle is unnecessary.

`npm run docs:generate` refreshes agent references, documentation discovery files, npm `AGENTS.md`,
and README guidance blocks. `npm run agents:check` validates frontmatter and reference links,
discovers and installs the checkout skill in a temporary project, and audits `npm pack --dry-run`.
It leaves consumer projects and the user's agent configuration untouched.

The entire `.agents/skills/rzmps` folder remains committed so GitHub installers can fetch it
without running a build. Its `SKILL.md` is generated from the definition below, and its reference
pages come from the guides, examples, and API declarations. Website indexes and `llms` files
are ignored build artifacts, regenerated for local builds and deployment. CI checks that the
committed skill matches its canonical sources; it does not automatically commit changes.

Run `npm run agents:check -- --github` to test the exact public shorthand discovery command.
CI checks GitHub commit URLs after pushes and the shorthand after publishing to the default
branch; pull requests validate their checkout without assuming the proposed skill is already public.

## Canonical Skill Definition

The following metadata and workflow generate `.agents/skills/rzmps/SKILL.md`. Edit them here;
the generated skill rewrites documentation links to bundled references so it remains portable.

<!-- skill:metadata:start -->
```yaml
name: rzmps
description: Build and debug Three.js particle systems and VFX in RZMPS using emitters, modules, renderers, and WebGL/WebGPU canvas previews.
```
<!-- skill:metadata:end -->

<!-- skill:instructions:start -->
Inspect the installed package version and public exports before using a feature. In this repository, use the current branch's TypeScript source. Prefer existing emitters, modules, renderers, and spatial effects before adding custom behavior.

Read [getting started](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-particle-system.html) for scene ownership and updates, [concepts](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/concepts.html) for lifecycle, priority, tags, spatial collections, and subsystem composition, and [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) before implementing TSL callbacks, readback, collision, or spatial-grid behavior. Search the [generated API](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/api/index.html) for signatures.

Reuse a canonical factory from `examples/`; inspect [example explanations](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/index.html) for its configuration rationale. Preserve the default factory and author metadata contracts. Add balanced documentation source regions and update the authored Markdown explanation, then run `npm run docs:generate` and `npm run docs:check`.

Check the selected renderer and custom material compatibility using [compatibility](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/compatibility.html). Build packages, run `npm run preview -- --example <id> --backend webgl`, and inspect the contact sheet and metadata. Repeat with webgpu when relevant; report unavailable backends explicitly. Adjust warmup, interval, or scene to capture the actual event. Technical success alone does not establish visual quality.

Update root systems once; parents own subsystem timing. Follow Module, Renderer, Emitter, and SpatialEffect CPU/GPU extension hooks and priority semantics. Do not treat WebGPU rendering as proof of GPU simulation; check component support and `isGPUProcessingActive`. Use features present in the installed version and current branch. Reference files are generated from human documentation; edit their canonical source instead.

Repository preview scripts and `examples/` are checkout tools. In a consumer project, adapt an example to its existing rendering loop or use a repository checkout for previews; do not assume consumers have repository npm scripts. Read the [installation guidance](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/ai-coding-assistants.html#installation) before installing the skill or changing agent configuration.
<!-- skill:instructions:end -->

# Benchmarks

These measurements describe one machine and browser, rather than a performance guarantee. Particle count, modules, geometry, resolution, and hardware all affect results. Simulation-only cases still run in a browser render loop; their particle renderer does no drawing.

## Running Benchmarks

From the repository root, install dependencies with `npm ci`, then run:

```sh
npm run benchmark:run
# Refresh the root and npm README tables from a new local measurement:
npm run benchmark:update-report
# Regenerate this page and the agent references from the README report:
npm run docs:generate
# Export a measurement without changing the published table:
npm run benchmark:export -- /tmp/rzmps-benchmark.json
```

The default run uses a headless, uncapped browser at 1280×720. Set `RZMPS_BENCHMARK_DURATION_MS` and `RZMPS_BENCHMARK_WARMUP_MS` to change measurement windows. Use `npm run benchmark:run -- --vsync` for browser frame pacing or `--headed` to view the run.

Average update time measures `ParticleSystem.update()`; frame time includes the render loop. The 1% low FPS is the reciprocal of the average of the slowest 1% of measured frames. P99 frame time is reported separately. The Particles column shows the measured population, with a minimum–maximum range for workloads such as spawn churn that change population during measurement.

## Pull Request Comparisons

CI builds and runs the complete benchmark page from each revision against its matching library. Three samples per revision run in interleaved ABBAAB order; the comparison uses the median for each metric and includes only case names present in both revisions.

GitHub-hosted runners use software WebGL. The CI profile uses a 640×360 viewport, browser frame pacing, and a 2,000-particle low polygon box workload for the mesh case. Its results are useful for relative comparisons on that runner and should be interpreted separately from the published hardware results above. Completed samples, environment metadata, and available timeout diagnostics are uploaded as workflow artifacts even when a run fails.

# Collision and Physics

The base package includes `ThreeCollisionBackend`, which raycasts against a
Three.js scene.

For GPU processing, `Collision` automatically selects `ThreeGPUCollisionBackend` when no backend
is supplied. It uses packed `three-mesh-bvh` acceleration data and distinguishes static,
transform-dynamic, and geometry-dynamic scene meshes. Supplying an explicit CPU physics backend
makes the collision module GPU-incompatible, and applying impulses to scene bodies remains a CPU
feature. See [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) before choosing an explicit backend.

See the generated API for constructor options and defaults.

The `ThreeCollisionBackend` uses two octrees for static and dynamic collisions.
Sorting objects into static and dynamic can be done automatically, or with
supporting identifiers passed into the constructor options. Explicitly stated
`staticObjects` and `dynamicObjects` lists are treated as the source of truth if
present.

If explicit lists are not provided, the scene is traversed and the
`staticObjectFilter`, `dynamicObjectFilter`, and `objectFilter` predicates are
used to select objects. `objectFilter` selects whether objects are included at
all but does not decide what is considered static or dynamic.

If none of these predicates are provided, the octrees are automatically
constructed from the scene traversal, with distinctions between static and
dynamic objects being made based on movement in the scene.

For external physics engines, use the extension packages:

| Package         | Engine       | npm                                                                            |
| --------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `@rzmps/rapier` | Rapier       | [npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/rapier](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/rapier) |
| `@rzmps/jolt`   | Jolt Physics | [npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/jolt](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/jolt)     |
| `@rzmps/ammo`   | Ammo.js      | [npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/ammo](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/ammo)     |

```ts
import { Collision } from "@rzmps/rzmps";
import { RapierCollisionBackend } from "@rzmps/rapier";

const collision = new Collision({
  backend: new RapierCollisionBackend({ RAPIER, world }),
  bounce: 0.6,
  dampen: 0.1,
  radiusScale: 1,
  lifetimeLoss: 0.2,
  applyImpulses: true,
});
```

Physics backends receive an existing physics world. They do not create, step, or
own the physics simulation.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/concepts.md -->

# Composition and Lifecycle

A `ParticleSystem` owns arrays of emitters, modules, renderers, and explicitly selected spatial effects. These are mutable collections; use `addEmitter`, `addModule`, `addRenderer`, and their removal methods when changing composition so setup and cleanup hooks run. Passing a single component to the constructor is also supported. Constructor options may be copied to instance fields, so changing an options object later does not always reconfigure a component. Check the exposed runtime property and its source before relying on live edits.

An emitter chooses where particles are born, their initial values, tags, and birth times. `rate` is particles per second; `rateOverDistance` adds emission based on source movement. A burst fires when its time is crossed. Lifetimes are seconds, while lifetime module callbacks receive normalized age from zero to one. A two-element array usually defines a sampled range; a `Set` selects a discrete value. Consult the exported dynamic-value types when supplying callbacks.

Each update restores cached permanent values, prepares modules once, sorts modifiers into priority phases, integrates particles, then sends the resulting particle list to renderers. [Module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) explains which changes persist. Renderers can share one simulated population: a sprite, trail, light, and sound can all represent the same particle. [Tags](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/tags.html) select subsets without duplicating simulation.

`start()` starts playback and resets the emission cycle, including when restarting a paused system. `pause()` freezes simulation. `stop(clearParticles)` stops emission and resets system time; surviving particles can continue moving on subsequent updates when they are retained. `destroy()` permanently releases owned resources. Removing a system from its scene performs temporary cleanup so it can be attached elsewhere. Call `destroy()` when you will no longer use it.

The loop duration schedules emission; it is independent of each particle's lifetime. Turning looping off does not necessarily delete existing particles: `endBehavior` determines what happens after the duration. A population estimate for constant emission is rate multiplied by average lifetime, before bursts, culling, or subsystems. These are nominal estimates: timestep quantization and emission scheduling can lower the observed count. Set `maxParticles` to bound simulation costs, and remember that each renderer adds work.

[Subsystems](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/subsystems.html) attach secondary effects to lifecycle events. [Spatial effects and collections](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/spatial-effects.html) coordinate scene-wide behavior. Both rendering backends use this same composition model; see [compatibility](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/compatibility.html) and [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html).

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/decals.md -->

# Surface Decals

`DecalRenderer` clips persistent geometry onto rigid scene meshes with Three.js `DecalGeometry`. Pass a material first and an optional options object. Each mark owns a material clone and geometry; your material, textures, and target geometry remain caller-owned. Standard Three.js materials work with WebGL and WebGPU rendering.

```ts
import * as THREE from 'three';
import { DecalRenderer } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: '#542710' });
const decals = new DecalRenderer(material, {
  direction: new THREE.Vector3(0, -1, 0),
  maxDistance: 2,
  depth: 0.1,
  size: 1,
  lifetime: 8,
  opacity: t => 1 - t,
});
// Supply decals in a ParticleSystem's renderers collection.
```

Spawn projection is enabled by default. Set `onSpawn: false, onCollision: true` for contact marks, or `onDeath: true` to search from the final particle position. Triggers are independent; enabling two can deliberately create two sets of marks for one particle. `continuousRate` defaults to zero (disabled). Set `onSpawn: false, continuousRate: 2` to project from each live particle twice per second instead of waiting for a collision. Its first projection occurs after one interval, so a particle that dies sooner than `1 / continuousRate` never projects continuously. Birth, collision, and death switches still work independently when continuous placement is enabled.

Continuous placement follows particle simulation age, respects tag filters, and stops when the particle dies. Pause freezes placement and decal aging; stopping emission without clearing lets surviving particles keep projecting. Repeated processing of the same particle snapshot does not duplicate an interval. If a large step crosses multiple intervals, missed projections use the current particle state, with catch-up work limited to `maxDecals` per particle per update. Clear/reset discard timing history; attaching to an already living population does not replay its entire past. Emitters, bursts, distance-based emission, and subsystems continue to determine which particles exist.

`ratio` defaults to `1` and is clamped to `[0, 1]`. It selects a consistent fraction of particles by ID for all projection triggers, including continuous placement. Setting it to zero disables new projections; existing decals continue fading.

Constructor settings are exposed directly as renderer properties, for example `decals.continuousRate = 2` or `decals.size = 1.5`; there is no stored options object. New configuration affects subsequent projections, while existing marks keep their creation-time properties. Numeric configuration is clamped instead of throwing: distance and depth remain positive, capacities/counts are rounded down, capacity/rate cannot be negative, and nonfinite values use defaults (or zero for an explicit invalid hit count). Radial ray counts are rounded down to at least one, with nonfinite counts becoming one.

Directions are world-space vectors. The exported `DecalDirectionSampler` and `DecalHitSelection` types describe direction and selection callbacks. A direction callback receives the original particle in its simulation space and may return one vector or an ordered array. Nonzero finite vectors are normalized without modifying them. `DecalRenderer.Radial(24)` returns twenty-four deterministic Fibonacci-sphere directions. Local particle positions are transformed into world space before querying.

`DecalRenderer.Forward()` samples local +Y transformed by `particle.rotation`, matching the forward-axis convention in `OrientToDirection`. Its optional `THREE.Vector3` supplies an XYZ rotation offset in radians, applied in the particle's local frame before its rotation. For example, rotate X by π to point backward:

```ts
const decals = new DecalRenderer(material, {
  direction: DecalRenderer.Forward(new THREE.Vector3(Math.PI, 0, 0)),
});
```

Forward follows orientation; use `OrientToDirection` when orientation should follow velocity. As with any particle-aware sampler, a rotated local simulation needs a callback that transforms the returned direction to world space using the system's world matrix. Samplers leave particle state and caller-owned vectors unchanged.

Each ray contributes its first supported intersection. Search uses a configured `ThreeCollisionBackend`'s current membership, including explicit object lists and filters; without that backend it scans scene meshes using the shared collision exclusions. Particle renderer objects and decal meshes are excluded. Other physics backends supply contacts directly when their `CollisionHit.object` is a supported mesh; otherwise search falls back to scene geometry. A valid collision contact bypasses direction sampling and raycasting. When mesh identity is unavailable, a finite nonzero collision normal selects the opposite world-space search direction, including on walls and slopes; the configured sampler is used only when that normal is unavailable. The built-in octree backend currently lacks target identity, so it uses this fallback, which can differ from an aggregate capsule contact.

`maxDistance` limits ray length in world units (default 2). `depth` is the projector's Z clipping thickness (default 0.1); width and height come from `size` and inherited X/Y scale. Normals use the mesh normal matrix, and particle Z rotation supplies projector roll in radians. `offset` displaces generated vertices along the outgoing normal (default 0.001). Keep depth shallow on thin or curved targets: clipping can reach nearby faces and corners can distort the projection.

`hitSelection` defaults to the direct callback `DecalRenderer.Nearest`. It receives `(hits, particle, maxHits)`, with `THREE.Intersection` candidates in ray order. `face.normal` and optional `normal` follow Three.js mesh-local conventions; transform them with the target's normal matrix for world-space comparisons.

| Selector | Omitted maxHits | Explicit maxHits: 4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DecalRenderer.Nearest` | One closest | Up to four closest |
| `DecalRenderer.Farthest` | One farthest | Up to four farthest |
| `DecalRenderer.All` | All in ray order | First four in ray order |

The built-ins leave the input array unchanged. Negative `maxHits` disables truncation; zero creates no marks. A custom selector may return fewer candidates. Explicit nonnegative `maxHits` also caps its valid result. Distinct intersections on one mesh remain separate candidates.

```ts
const decals = new DecalRenderer(material, {
  direction: DecalRenderer.Radial(24),
  maxHits: 4,
  hitSelection: (hits, particle, maxHits) => {
    const upward = hits.filter(hit => {
      const normal = (hit.normal ?? hit.face?.normal)?.clone();
      if (!normal) return false;
      normal.applyMatrix3(new THREE.Matrix3().getNormalMatrix(hit.object.matrixWorld)).normalize();
      return normal.y > 0.5;
    });
    return DecalRenderer.Nearest(upward, particle, maxHits);
  },
});
```

`color` accepts `ColorInput` values (Three.js colors, CSS strings, or numeric hex values). `size` accepts `Vector3Input`: a number for uniform width/height or a vector for separate X/Y dimensions; Z is ignored because `depth` controls clipping. Both support callbacks, ranges, and sets without modifying caller-owned values.

`size`, `color`, and `lifetime` use the existing CPU `DynamicValue` helpers and are sampled once at source particle age. Geometry never resizes after creation. Nonpositive or nonfinite lifetime/size creates nothing. Lifetime is in seconds; its default is eight. `opacity` is evaluated on normalized **decal age** from zero to one, with a stable source seed for random ranges. It multiplies the template material opacity and snapshotted alpha. CPU evaluation does not accept TSL nodes.

`inheritColor`, `inheritScale`, and `inheritAlpha` default to 1 and follow subsystem math: base multiplied by `lerp(1, particleValue, amount)`, component-wise for color and nonuniform scale. Zero and negative amounts retain the base value, matching subsystem handling. Half blends halfway, and one inherits fully. The material color, configured color, and inherited particle color multiply together. Each decal's material fades independently.

`distanceAffectsSize` and `distanceAffectsOpacity` default to zero. Their multiplier is `lerp(1, proximity, amount)`, where `proximity = 1 - clamp(hit.distance / maxDistance, 0, 1)`. Zero is neutral and one gives full distance attenuation.

`maxHits` limits selection per trigger. `maxDecals` instead limits active persistent marks (default 256). Insertion at capacity evicts the oldest mark and disposes its geometry and cloned material. Expiry, `clear`, reset, removal from the scene, and destruction also release owned resources. Pause freezes decal age; stopping without clearing lets marks continue fading. Destruction unregisters callbacks. Renderer update/count LOD does not skip lifetime updates or lifecycle placement; tag filters still apply. Normal system simulation LOD and culling affect the system clock as usual.

Generated geometry is stored in the target mesh's local space so it follows rigid motion. Skinned and instanced targets are rejected; deforming geometry and animated morph targets are unsupported. Choose a material with a color property when using tint inheritance. Texture and custom shader compatibility follow the supplied material's capabilities.

GPU event-only modes use the existing asynchronous lifecycle-event snapshots without adding particle readbacks. Continuous mode uses the same `updateCPUFromGPU` helper as LightRenderer and TrailRenderer, forwarding snapshots through the normal update path. There is no separate readback-frequency cap; the helper guards against overlapping requests. Fixed direction vectors request position, rotation, normalized age, and elapsed age, plus scale/color/alpha when inherited. Arbitrary direction callbacks may inspect every particle field, so those request complete snapshots. Decal lifetimes still advance on each simulation update while a readback is in flight. Marks may appear after readback latency. GPU contacts currently lack mesh identity and search opposite the collision normal. Follow-up work: preserve GPU collision target identity for exact contact projection. Geometry clipping and material allocation remain CPU work; batching and deforming mesh projection are deferred.

The [Splatter example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/splatter.html) uses matte paintballs and long-lived collision marks that inherit color and scale. The [Fire example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fire.html) uses continuous radial projection from its flame particles. Short-lived, low-opacity marks fade in and accumulate into textured scorch patches. [Fireball](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireball.html) uses the same texture with a higher continuous rate suited to its brief bursts.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/development.md -->

# Local Development

Clone the repository and install dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps.git
cd rzmps
npm install
```

Run the demo and documentation together, with package watchers:

```bash
npm run dev
```

The command generates the documentation sources and builds the packages, then serves
the demo at `http://localhost:5173/`. Preview images are generated while the demo is
available. Documentation starts at `http://localhost:5173/docs/` once previews finish.
During preview generation, documentation requests return a temporary 503 response.

Use `npm run docs:dev` for the same startup sequence without package watchers.
`npm run docs:generate` still generates both documentation sources and previews;
`npm run docs:generate -- --skip-previews` defers previews to `npm run docs:previews`.

Preview images and their manifest in `apps/docs/public/previews/` are ignored build
artifacts. Documentation builds regenerate missing or stale previews using Puppeteer;
CI installs Chrome before building. Local captures are reused while their inputs match.

Build the core package:

```bash
npm run build --workspace packages/rzmps
```

Run the package in watch mode:

```bash
npm run dev --workspace packages/rzmps
```

Run the demo locally:

```bash
npm start --workspace apps/demo
```

Build the demo:

```bash
npm run build --workspace apps/demo
```

Build the physics extensions:

```bash
npm run build --workspace @rzmps/rapier
npm run build --workspace @rzmps/jolt
npm run build --workspace @rzmps/ammo
```

Build all publishable packages:

```bash
npm run build:modules
```

Run the core library regression tests:

```bash
npm test
```

The test suite lives in `packages/rzmps/tests` and focuses on behavior that is
easy to regress while optimizing internals: force application, priority phases,
depth and size mapping, distortion controls, audio effect calculations,
mutable-value isolation, and subsystem inheritance.

Run the benchmark suite and print browser-rendered results to the terminal:

```bash
npm run benchmark:run
```

Benchmark runs disable browser frame-rate limiting by default. Add `-- --vsync`
to measure refresh-rate-bound behavior instead.

Open a visible browser window while running the same benchmark:

```bash
npm run benchmark:run -- --open
```

Serve the built benchmark page for visual/manual inspection:

```bash
npm run benchmark:serve --workspace demo
```

Then open `http://127.0.0.1:4173/?benchmark=1`.

Update the benchmark report tables in the READMEs:

```bash
npm run benchmark:update-report
```

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/dynamic-values.md -->

# Dynamic Values

Many RZMPS options use `DynamicValue<T>`.

```ts
type DynamicValue<T> =
  | T
  | ((t: number) => DynamicValue<T>)
  | [DynamicValue<T>, DynamicValue<T>]
  | Set<DynamicValue<T>>;

// Used for parameters that can take multiple elements or just one
type Multiple<T> = T | T[];

// Multiple with least one value
type StrictMultiple<T> = T | [T, ...[T]];

// In RZMPS, tags are natively strings
type Tag = string;
```

Lifetime-module callbacks receive normalized particle age, from `0` to `1`. Emitter rate and birth-value callbacks instead receive normalized emission-cycle time. A callback is evaluated in its component’s context; it does not receive wall-clock seconds.

| Form           | Example                       | Behavior                               |
| -------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Static value   | `2`                           | Always returns the same value.         |
| Function       | `(t) => 1 - t`                | Re-evaluates over normalized lifetime. |
| Two-item array | `[0.5, 2]`                    | Random value between min and max.      |
| Set            | `new Set(["spark", "smoke"])` | Random choice.                         |

Dynamic values are supported for numbers, vectors, and colors where the option
type uses `DynamicValue<number>`, `DynamicValue<THREE.Vector3>`, or
`DynamicValue<THREE.Color>`.

Color inputs accept `THREE.Color`, hex numbers, and CSS color strings (the same values
as `new THREE.Color(...)`). Uniform-axis inputs such as scale, scale velocity/acceleration,
noise strength, and velocity limits also accept a number: `scale: 2` means
`new THREE.Vector3(2, 2, 2)`. Positions and directional inputs still require vectors.
These shortcuts work inside callbacks, ranges, and sets too, including GPU processing;
particle state always contains `THREE.Color` and `THREE.Vector3` objects.

```ts
initialValues: {
  color: new Set(["#ff8844", 0xffcc00]),
  scale: [0.1, 0.5],
}
// Lifetime modifier: scale: (t) => 1 + t
```

The [curves](https://www.npmjs.com/package/curves) package was designed and
built to streamline functional values by defining and evaluating eased curves,
similar to Unity's AnimationCurves with modifiers akin to Blender's FCurve
Modifiers. It has prebuilt keyframe types for numbers, colors, and vectors,
compatible with the `THREE.Vector3` and `THREE.Color` types.


## Parameter-Based Values

Depth, size, and speed modules use `ValueByParameter<T>` rather than random dynamic ranges.
A two-element array interpolates between its endpoints using the normalized parameter.
A direct numeric or vector value scales with that parameter; a function returns its explicit
result. For example, `[0.5, 2]` interpolates from 0.5 to 2, while `() => 2` supplies a constant
result. Check the option's actual type before assuming an array means random sampling.

Random lifetime values are often evaluated with a particle ID seed, so a particle keeps
its sampled choice across repeated module updates. Emitter birth sampling selects new
values for new particles. Do not mutate a vector supplied as a shared option inside a
custom callback; update the particle's own state or reuse a separate scratch vector.

GPU built-ins support the same constant, range, set, and callback forms. Function values are
sampled into an interpolated lookup table with `ParticleSystem.GPU_DYNAMIC_VALUE_RESOLUTION`
entries, so sharp or high-frequency curves may need a higher resolution. GPU-aware options can
also accept TSL nodes. Runtime value changes synchronize automatically; a change that alters a
custom shader graph's structure should additionally set that component's `needsUpdate` flag.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.md -->

# First GPU Module

A custom module needs a CPU callback and a TSL callback to behave on both simulation backends.
This example adds the same upward acceleration in each path.

```ts
import { Module, ParticleSystem } from "@rzmps/rzmps";
import { float, vec3 } from "three/tsl";

const updraft = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime) => {
    particle.velocity.y += 0.5 * deltaTime;
  },
  {
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime) => {
      const acceleration = vec3(0, float(0.5).mul(deltaTime), 0);
      particle.velocity.assign(particle.velocity.add(acceleration));
    },
  },
);

const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters,
  modules: [updraft],
  renderers,
  gpuProcessing: true,
});
```

The CPU callback runs once for each JavaScript particle. The GPU callback runs while RZMPS builds
a compute graph: its particle properties and `deltaTime` are TSL nodes, not current JavaScript
values. Build expressions with TSL functions and write fields with `assign`; JavaScript arithmetic
or branching cannot inspect a node's per-particle value.

The two callbacks should express the same behavior, but they need not use identical algorithms.
`supportsGPU` is true only when `modifyGPU` exists and every custom CPU condition has a matching
`conditionGPU`. After the renderer initializes, use `particles.isGPUProcessingActive` to check the
backend actually selected.

## Conditions and Spatial Queries

A custom CPU `condition` also needs a TSL equivalent:

```ts
const risingOnly = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime) => {
    particle.velocity.y += 0.5 * deltaTime;
  },
  {
    condition: (particle) => particle.velocity.y > 0,
    conditionGPU: (particle) => particle.velocity.y.greaterThan(0),
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime) => {
      particle.velocity.y.addAssign(float(0.5).mul(deltaTime));
    },
  },
);
```

## Managed Spatial Grid

The GPU counterpart to a managed octree is `ParticleSpatialGrid`. This version of the crowd-drag
module uses the grid's exact-radius query and performs the count entirely in the compute graph:

```ts
const crowdDrag = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, _system, octree) => {
    const nearbyCount = octree
      .particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2)
      .filter((neighbor) => neighbor !== particle)
      .length;
    particle.velocity.multiplyScalar(
      Math.max(0, 1 - nearbyCount * 0.02 * deltaTime),
    );
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    octreeOptions: { maxDepth: 6, particlesPerLeaf: 8 },
    useSpatialGrid: true,
    spatialGridOptions: { brickSubdivisions: 3, cellSubdivisions: 4 },
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime, _context, grid) => {
      if (!grid) return;

      const nearbyCount = float(0).toVar("nearbyCount");
      grid.forEachParticleInRadius(
        particle.position,
        float(2),
        () => nearbyCount.addAssign(1),
        { excludeIndex: particle.index },
      );
      const damping = float(1)
        .sub(nearbyCount.mul(0.02).mul(deltaTime))
        .max(0);
      particle.velocity.mulAssign(damping);
    },
  },
);
```

RZMPS rebuilds both structures and passes the appropriate one as the final callback argument. A
grid query emits shader-side work and never returns JavaScript particles. Its callback can inspect
each neighbor and the squared distance when a count alone is not enough. Keep query bounds and
grid resolution appropriate for the effect; see
[particle spatial acceleration](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/particle-octree.html) for configuration and limitations.

Runtime scalar, vector, color, range, and curve properties on built-in modules synchronize to GPU
parameters automatically. A custom class can use its protected `gpuParameters` store for the same
pattern. Set `needsUpdate = true` only when a change alters graph structure or owned resources.

Continue with [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) for execution phases, fallback rules, readback,
and validation.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.md -->

# First GPU Spatial Effect

A custom spatial effect pairs its ordinary particle modifier with `modifyGPU`. Built-in volume
factories provide the CPU inclusion test and GPU influence calculation automatically.

```ts
import { ParticleSystem, SpatialEffect } from "@rzmps/rzmps";
import { float, vec3 } from "three/tsl";

const updraft = SpatialEffect.Sphere(
  (particle, deltaTime, _system, strength) => {
    particle.velocity.y += 2 * deltaTime * strength;
  },
  {
    automaticFeather: false,
    feather: 0.75,
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime, _context, strength) => {
      const acceleration = vec3(0, float(2).mul(deltaTime).mul(strength), 0);
      particle.velocity.assign(particle.velocity.add(acceleration));
    },
  },
  2,
  24,
  16,
);

updraft.position.set(0, 1, 0);
scene.add(updraft);

const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters,
  modules,
  renderers,
  gpuProcessing: true,
});
scene.add(particles);
```

With `automaticFeather: false`, both callbacks receive a strength from zero through one, so the
example applies feathering explicitly and identically. With automatic feathering enabled, RZMPS
blends supported particle fields around the callback instead.

`SpatialEffect.Sphere`, `Box`, `Cone`, and `Torus` supply matching built-in CPU and GPU tests. Add
`conditionGPU` only when adding a custom CPU `condition`. Add `testGPU` when replacing the volume's
inclusion rule with a custom `test`; it returns a float influence rather than a JavaScript boolean.
Custom geometry without `testGPU` uses a baked influence field.

Spatial effects are scene objects. Their transforms can move while
`updatePolicy: SpatialEffectUpdatePolicy.TransformDynamic` updates transform data without
rebuilding geometry acceleration. Use `GeometryDynamic` only when vertex data itself changes.
Custom tests are not bounds-filtered because RZMPS cannot assume they depend on the effect's
geometry.

After the renderer initializes, verify `particles.isGPUProcessingActive`. Unsupported generic
spatial effects are skipped by GPU simulation instead of forcing the entire system onto CPU, so
also inspect each custom effect's `supportsGPU` while developing it. See
[GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) for batching, invalidation, and profiling.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-module.md -->

# First Module

Modules change particle values over time. A custom module receives the live
particle, the frame delta, and the owning particle system.

```ts
import { Module } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const riseAndFade = new Module((particle, deltaTime) => {
  particle.velocity.y += 0.5 * deltaTime;
  particle.alpha *= 1 - particle.time;
});
```

Attach it to a system with the rest of your modules:

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters,
  modules: [riseAndFade],
  renderers,
});
```

Use `condition` when only some particles should be affected:

```ts
const sparksOnly = new Module((particle) => {
  particle.scale.multiplyScalar(1.2);
}, {
  condition: (particle) => particle.tags?.includes("spark") ?? false,
});
```

The exported `ModuleCondition` type receives the same arguments as `ModuleUpdate`:
`(particle, deltaTime, particleSystem?, octree?)`, and returns a boolean. The system and managed
octree are optional, just as they are for the update callback. Conditions run after alive and tag
filtering and receive the same frame delta and context as the update. Existing particle-only
predicates still work. On GPU, `ModuleGPUCondition` matches `ModuleGPUUpdate`'s arguments and
returns a TSL boolean node.

For performance-sensitive modules, avoid allocating objects inside the per
particle callback. Reuse vectors and colors outside the callback when possible.

A plain Module defaults to permanent priority. The example's velocity increment accumulates over time; multiplying by delta seconds makes 0.5 an acceleration rather than an amount per frame. Its alpha multiplication also accumulates. For a fade defined entirely by normalized age, prefer ColorOverLifetime or set `priority: Module.Priority.Transient` so the fade is reapplied to cached base alpha each frame.

Use `Module.Priority.PreMovementTransient` when a temporary velocity adjustment must affect this frame's integration. Render-time transient modules run after movement. See [module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) before combining several modules that assign the same property.

## Managed Octree

Particle-to-particle comparisons should use a managed `ParticleOctree` instead of scanning the
whole particle array for every particle. Enable it in the module options; RZMPS rebuilds it and
passes it as the callback's fourth argument.

```ts
const crowdDrag = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, _system, octree) => {
    const nearbyCount = octree
      .particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2)
      .filter((neighbor) => neighbor !== particle)
      .length;
    const damping = Math.max(0, 1 - nearbyCount * 0.02 * deltaTime);
    particle.velocity.multiplyScalar(damping);
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    octreeOptions: {
      maxDepth: 6,
      particlesPerLeaf: 8,
    },
  },
);
```

The octree owns its default aggregator, which returns an empty object for every node.
Supply `octreeAggregator` when a module needs custom aggregate data, such as a count or average velocity.

The octree prunes nodes outside the query sphere, then returns the particles that pass exact
distance checks in the remaining leaves. Custom aggregate data remains useful when an
approximation such as average position or velocity is cheaper than collecting every matching
particle; see
[particle spatial acceleration](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/particle-octree.html).

For reusable behavior, extend Module and pass your per-particle callback and options to `super`. Override `prepare(system, deltaTime)` when expensive shared work should happen once per frame; call `super.prepare` if using automatic spatial-effect collection. Put resource cleanup in `cleanup()`. Dependencies in `dependents` participate in normal priority sorting rather than forcing an independent update loop.

Built-in modules already cover forces, noise, scale, rotation, depth, color, and collision. Reuse those when their semantics match the effect. Custom callbacks are most useful for application-specific logic, and should mutate the particle provided rather than storing a shared mutable vector in multiple particles.

The callback above is CPU-only. Continue with [First GPU Module](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.html) to add the
equivalent TSL operation, then use [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) as the reference for managed
spatial queries, invalidation, and testing requirements.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-spatial-effect.md -->

# First Spatial Effect

Spatial effects modify particles based on scene-space volumes or custom tests.
Use a built-in force field when particles should react to an area in the scene.

```ts
import * as THREE from "three";
import { ParticleForceField } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const updraft = ParticleForceField.Sphere({
  direction: new THREE.Vector3(0, 2, 0),
}, 2);

updraft.position.set(0, 1, 0);
scene.add(updraft);
```

Particle systems discover generic spatial effects in their scene by default.
Disable that behavior per system with `useSpatialEffects: false`, or use
`spatialEffectFilter` to choose which effects apply.

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  spatialEffectFilter: (effect) => effect.name === "updraft",
});
```

Use `KillZone` when particles should be removed inside a volume:

```ts
import { KillZone } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const cleanup = KillZone.Box(10, 4, 10);
cleanup.position.y = -3;
scene.add(cleanup);
```

Name the updraft (`updraft.name = 'updraft'`) before using the filter shown above. A filter cannot find an unnamed field by that name. The direction vector supplies acceleration while the field applies its timestep. In custom callbacks, multiply acceleration by deltaTime before adding it to velocity.

For a custom volume modifier, use `SpatialEffect.Box((particle, deltaTime) => { ... }, options, width, height, depth)`. Scale and position it like another Object3D. A custom `test` option can replace the geometric inclusion rule, while `inverted` applies to the opposite side of a volume. Choose a permanent priority for forces and a transient priority for temporary color or scale changes.

Scene discovery and module-level collections serve different purposes. A generic field modifies intersecting particles directly; a specialized affector can instead be collected by a module such as Boids. See [spatial collections](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/spatial-effects.html) for explicit selection and filtering, and [module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) for execution phases.

Custom CPU callbacks do not translate into shader code. Continue with
[First GPU Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.html) to pair this volume with a TSL modifier,
then use [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) as the reference for batching and moving-geometry
policies.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/gpu-processing.md -->

# GPU Processing and Extension Development

RZMPS keeps the same `ParticleSystem` composition on CPU and GPU: emitters create particles,
modules and spatial effects modify them, and renderers display them. Set `gpuProcessing: true`
(the default) and render the system once with an initialized Three.js `WebGPURenderer` to make
GPU simulation eligible. `isGPUProcessingActive` reports the backend actually selected for the
current system; `gpuProcessing` only expresses the requested mode.

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters: [emitter],
  modules: [force, color],
  renderers: [sprites],
  gpuProcessing: true,
});

scene.add(particles);
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  particles.update();
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
});
```

WebGL always uses CPU simulation. A WebGPU system also uses CPU simulation when GPU processing is
disabled, a module lacks a GPU implementation, GPU tag capacity is exceeded, or a CPU-input
renderer is combined with a render-time modifier. Unsupported generic spatial effects are skipped
by the GPU path rather than moving the entire system to CPU. Inspect `supportsGPU`,
`getGPUEmissionSupport()`, `getGPUExecutionSchedule()`, and `isGPUProcessingActive` when composing
custom components. Changing `gpuProcessing` starts a fresh run because CPU objects and GPU buffers
are separate authoritative states.

## Writing CPU and GPU Modules

The CPU callback mutates a JavaScript `Particle`. `modifyGPU` builds a Three.js Shading Language
(TSL) graph over a `GPUParticleLike`; it does not execute once per particle in JavaScript. Work
through [First GPU Module](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.html) for a complete paired implementation and
[First GPU Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.html) for influence, feathering, and custom test
rules.

Reuse ordinary CPU hooks for setup and cleanup. `prepare(system, deltaTime)` runs once before a
module's work on either backend. A function-defined module can request managed acceleration with
`useOctree`/`octreeOptions` for CPU or `useSpatialGrid`/`spatialGridOptions` for GPU; the resulting
`ParticleOctree` or `ParticleSpatialGrid` is passed as the optional final callback argument.
`cleanup()` must call `super.cleanup()` when overridden so managed references are released.

`ParticleSpatialGrid` hashes occupied fine cells; it does not allocate a dense world-volume grid.
Its cached build kernels dispatch over `buffers.count`, not reserved capacity, and are submitted
together. A compact GPU-produced population can pass a `GPUComputeRange` as the fourth argument to
`rebuild(renderer, buffers, buildToken, range)`. The range pairs a uint count node with caller-owned
indirect compute arguments (`ceil(count / 64), 1, 1`), written by an earlier GPU scheduling pass.
No count readback is required. `grid.computeParticles(callback, range)` reuses that dispatch
contract for additional kernels, including exact partial-workgroup guarding. Without a range,
the returned kernel uses the current CPU count; update its `count` when that population changes.
Callbacks decide whether dead slots participate. These kernels require an initialized grid and
must be rebuilt if the grid's underlying particle storage is replaced.

### Spatial Aggregation And Levels

`SpatialAggregator<T, "cpu">` preserves the octree's existing `new` and `combine` members
and optionally adds `finalize`. Parent reductions retain raw values. `getAggregate(node)`
finalizes a copy, so deriving averages does not overwrite sums used by other nodes.
CPU values remain ordinary objects; they do not require GPU layouts. Keep finalized state
copyable; native data containers, ordinary object graphs and classes with `clone()` are supported.

`SpatialAggregator<Layout, "gpu">` uses the same concepts with explicit channel types and
TSL expressions. Layout channels support `float`, `uint`, `int`, `vec2`, `vec3` and `vec4`.
Combine raw sums/counts associatively; derive means or normalized vectors in `finalize`.
GPU finalization operates on local expressions, leaving stored raw reductions intact.

```ts
const grid = new ParticleSpatialGrid({ levels: SpatialLevels.All }, {
  layout: { count: 'uint', sum: 'vec3' },
  new: particle => ({
    count: uint(particle ? 1 : 0),
    sum: particle?.position ?? vec3(0),
  }),
  combine: (a, b) => ({ count: a.count.add(b.count), sum: a.sum.add(b.sum) }),
  finalize: a => ({ count: a.count, sum: a.sum.div(float(a.count).max(1)) }),
});
grid.rebuild(renderer, buffers);
const readRegions = grid.computeRegions(0, region => {
  const average = grid.getAggregate(region);
  const bounds = grid.getBounds(region);
  const children = grid.getChildren(region);
  // Consume these GPU expressions in your compute graph; they are not synchronous CPU values.
});
```

Import the TSL constructors from `three/tsl`, and `ParticleSpatialGrid`/`SpatialLevels`
from RZMPS. GPU aggregate callbacks construct graphs, not JavaScript particle callbacks.
The fixed layout and callbacks are construction-time configuration; use captured uniforms
for runtime numeric tuning. Callers own and dispose compute kernels returned by the grid.

Let B be `brickSubdivisions` and D be B plus `cellSubdivisions`:

| `levels` | Maintained depths |
| --- | --- |
| `SpatialLevels.None` / `"none"` / `"None"`, default | D only |
| `SpatialLevels.Bricks` / `"bricks"` / `"Bricks"` | 0 through B, plus D |
| `SpatialLevels.Cells` / `"cells"` / `"Cells"` | B through D |
| `SpatialLevels.All` / `"*"` / `"All"` | 0 through D |
| Readonly integer array | Requested depths plus D, sorted and deduplicated |

Both brick/cell presets include B. Invalid depths or presets throw rather than silently
clamping. The finest neighbor-query index is always present. Ordinary default/None grids
without an aggregator allocate no extra region directories. A non-None preset, explicit
depth array, or aggregator enables the optional sparse region directory; aggregate storage
is allocated only when an aggregator is supplied. Managed grids share only compatible levels.

Region handles are frame-local GPU expressions with a `valid` flag. `locateNode(position, depth)`
finds an occupied region at a maintained depth; outside or empty regions are invalid.
`getRegions(depth)` gives a GPU count and ordinal-to-region accessor; `computeRegions`
dispatches only occupied regions. Requesting an unmaintained depth throws, rather than reporting
an empty level. `getChildren` means the **next maintained finer level**, not necessarily depth+1.
Repeat child traversal to reach occupied descendants without scanning every region at that depth.
At the finest level, `getParticleIndices` gives the region's particle membership range.

CPU octree handles are ordinary node references. Its existing `locate` returns the deepest
available containing node up to the requested depth, with the existing root fallback outside
bounds; grid `locate(Vector3, depth)` remains a CPU coordinate utility, not a GPU lookup.
Both structures provide `getAggregate`, `getBounds` and `getChildren` where those concepts agree.
Neither node references nor GPU region indices should be retained across rebuilds.

Additional grid levels use exact sparse cell keys, compact occupied-cell lists and child
ranges. The finest summaries are constructed once; coarser levels combine raw child summaries.
No dense world-volume arrays or separate pointer-based GPU octree are constructed. Hash-table
capacity clearing remains allocation-sized, while scans and aggregate work use occupied counts.

Dynamic numbers, vectors, colors, ranges, sets, and callbacks are available to built-in GPU
components. Callback curves are sampled into interpolated uniform tables at
`ParticleSystem.GPU_DYNAMIC_VALUE_RESOLUTION`; increase it when a high-frequency curve needs more
fidelity. TSL nodes can be supplied directly where a dynamic value is evaluated by GPU code.

## Emitters and Spatial Effects

Built-in GPU emission supports rate, distance rate, timed bursts, tags, initial values, LOD, and
volume, surface, or vertex sampling from buffer geometry. CPU and GPU volume emission share the
shape's baked Halton sample table. `volumeSamples` is `"auto"` by default; assigning a number fixes
the table size, while changing geometry or the sample setting rebuilds it. Surface selection is
weighted by triangle area. Burst times are normalized emission-cycle values from 0 through 1.

Emitters use the built-in GPU birth pipeline; they are configured through `Emitter` and
`EmissionShape`, not extended with a separate shader callback. Custom behavior belongs in a
module or spatial effect after birth.

Custom `SpatialEffect` implementations pair the CPU `modify`, `condition`, and `test` callbacks
with `modifyGPU`, `conditionGPU`, and `testGPU`. The GPU test returns a float influence from 0 to 1,
which supplies feather strength to `modifyGPU`. Built-in analytic volumes are batched and indexed.
Custom geometry uses a baked field, controlled by `bakedFieldResolution`; set `updatePolicy` to
`Static`, `TransformDynamic`, or `GeometryDynamic` when automatic change detection is not the best
fit. Custom tests are not bounds-filtered because RZMPS cannot assume they depend on geometry.

## Renderers, Events, and Readback

GPU-native renderers override `_updateGPU` and consume `GPUParticleBufferState` or the compact
render-output buffer. A renderer whose implementation needs ordinary `Particle` objects can
override `_updateGPU` and call the protected `updateCPUFromGPU` helper. It selectively reads the
requested fields, ignores overlapping requests while one is pending, and passes the resulting
particles through the renderer's public `update` method. Override `updateGPUUsesCPUReadback` to
keep child expansion on that CPU path:

```ts
class DebugRenderer extends Renderer {
  get updateGPUUsesCPUReadback() { return true; }

  _updateGPU(buffers, system, deltaTime) {
    this.updateCPUFromGPU(
      buffers,
      system,
      deltaTime,
      64,
      ["position", "color", "alpha"],
    );
  }

  _update(particles) {
    // Render the selectively reconstructed Particle objects.
  }
}
```

Request only the slots and fields the renderer actually consumes. Outside a renderer, use the
public system API directly:

```ts
const samples = await system.selectiveReadback(64, ["position", "color", "alpha"]);
```

Readback is delayed and may return no result if its bounded pool is busy. Do not use it to drive
same-frame simulation decisions. Lifecycle and collision events are also delivered asynchronously
from GPU buffers, so listeners and CPU audio/render views can lag simulation slightly. GPU-native
subsystems consume spawn, death, collision, and continuous emission on the GPU; update only the
root system, as on CPU.

Native subsystem births stay within WebGPU's default limit of eight compute-stage storage-buffer
bindings. Parent and child particle state each use separate float and integer buffers. The
remaining pass-specific bindings come from packed allocation state, the emitter-runtime fields
actually referenced by that pass, and packed shape-sampling data. Emitters dispatch separately so
adding emitters does not accumulate their geometry bindings in one shader. Applications do not
need to request a higher device limit.

## Collision and Neighbor Queries

`Collision` selects `ThreeCollisionBackend` for CPU processing and `ThreeGPUCollisionBackend` for
GPU processing when no backend is supplied. An explicit CPU-only backend makes the module GPU
incompatible. GPU collision does not support applying impulses back to scene bodies. Classify GPU
geometry with `CollisionGeometryUpdatePolicy`: static geometry is built once, transform-dynamic
geometry updates transforms, and geometry-dynamic meshes refit or rebuild changed acceleration
data.

Use `ParticleOctree` for CPU neighbor work and `ParticleSpatialGrid` for GPU queries. A grid query
emits TSL and invokes its visitor in shader code; it does not return JavaScript particles. Bounds
can expand automatically, but a larger volume lowers spatial resolution because the logical cell
count stays fixed. `maxQuerySteps: 0` performs unbounded exact traversal; a positive value is an
explicit performance cap.

## Configuration and Validation

Built-in components synchronize ordinary runtime property changes before each GPU frame. Constant
and sampled value changes update uniforms; structural changes invalidate and rebuild the affected
compute graph or resources. Custom components should expose changed scalar/vector data through
their GPU parameter nodes and set `needsUpdate = true` when changing graph structure, geometry
layout, callback identity, or buffer ownership.

Test both execution paths. WebGPU rendering alone does not prove GPU simulation is active: assert
`isGPUProcessingActive` after rendering has captured its context. Compare CPU and GPU behavior at
fixed timesteps, exercise resets and subsystem events, and inspect `gpuBufferStats`,
`gpuEventStats`, `gpuSpatialStats`, `gpuSelectiveReadbackStats`, and `gpuConfigurationStats` when
profiling. GPU output is expected to be behaviorally equivalent, not bit-for-bit identical.

See [renderer children and population LOD](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/renderer-children-lod.html) for system quality, destructive culling, visual expansion, hierarchy access, and default GPU buffer limits.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/module-priority.md -->

# Module Priority and Execution Order

RZMPS sorts modules and generic spatial effects together by numeric priority. Smaller priorities run first within a phase. Input order is preserved for equal priorities. A module's `dependents` are flattened before sorting; each dependent's own priority still determines its phase.

| Priority | Phase | Persistence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Less than 0 | Before movement | Changes become permanent simulation state |
| 0 up to, excluding, 1 | Before movement | Transient changes influence this frame's movement |
| 1 or greater | After movement | Transient changes affect this frame's rendered appearance |

Use `Module.Priority.Permanent` (`-1`) for acceleration or accumulated changes. Multiply acceleration by `deltaTime` so the change is expressed per second. Use `Module.Priority.PreMovementTransient` (`0.5`) for a temporary velocity adjustment that should influence integration without accumulating into next frame's base velocity. Use `Module.Priority.Transient` (`1`) for a size or tint multiplier derived from normalized particle age.

At the beginning of the next update, cached values are restored. A render-time velocity change therefore does not move the particle in the current frame, and it does not automatically become next frame's velocity. This is why changing the priority can change the meaning of an otherwise identical callback.

Prefer a built-in lifetime module before writing an equivalent callback: those modules already select phases appropriate to their behavior. When combining modifiers that write the same property, inspect both their priorities and whether each callback assigns or multiplies that property. A later assignment can replace an earlier result.

`prepare(system, deltaTime)` runs before the per-particle phase. Use it for shared calculations or spatial collection, and reuse scratch objects in the particle callback. Population LOD removes simulated particles before module work; surviving particles run every step.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/particle-octree.md -->

# Particle Spatial Acceleration

RZMPS provides complementary structures for particle-to-particle work:

| Operation | `ParticleOctree` (CPU) | `ParticleSpatialGrid` (GPU) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bounds | `setBounds`, `bounds` | `setBounds`, `bounds` |
| Resolution | `maxDepth`, `particlesPerLeaf` | `maxDepth`, brick/cell subdivisions |
| Update | `rebuild(particles, tags?)` | `rebuild(renderer, buffers, token?)` |
| Position lookup | `locate(position)` returns a node | `locate(position)` returns a cell coordinate |
| Radius query | `particlesInRadius` array | `forEachParticleInRadius` TSL visitor |
| Quality | `timeQuality` | `timeQuality` |
| Cleanup | garbage-collected CPU data | `dispose(renderer?)` / `destroy(renderer?)` |

Use `ParticleOctree` for CPU comparisons, neighborhood queries, and aggregate approximations. Use
`ParticleSpatialGrid` for GPU comparisons and exact-radius shader queries. They share conceptual
configuration names where the meanings match, but their results are intentionally different:
octree queries return CPU particle arrays and expose aggregates, while grid queries emit shader work and never
materialize a JavaScript particle array.

## CPU: ParticleOctree

`ParticleOctree<TAggregate>` groups particle positions into cubic cells and computes an application-defined aggregate. It supports exact-radius queries as well as aggregate approximations. It is separate from mesh collision acceleration: its entries are particle indices, not triangle faces.

Supply a configuration and an aggregator with `new` and `combine` functions. `new` must handle an absent particle because the tree asks it for an empty node aggregate. `combine` merges aggregates; return independent state or carefully manage mutation so sibling nodes cannot corrupt one another.

```ts
import { ParticleOctree } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const tree = new ParticleOctree<number>({
  maxDepth: 6,
  particlesPerLeaf: 8,
  timeQuality: 1,
}, {
  new: (particle) => particle ? 1 : 0,
  combine: (a, b) => a + b,
});

tree.setBounds(system.boundingBox);
tree.rebuild(system.particles);
const node = tree.locate(system.particles[0].position);
const neighbors = tree.particlesInRadius(
  system.particles[0].position,
  2,
  { excludeIndex: 0 },
);
```

Guard the last line when the population is empty. `rebuild` accepts an optional tag selection. Only particles inside the resolved bounds and matching that selection contribute. Choose bounds in the same coordinate space as particle positions. Call `setBounds` when your population moves beyond the original volume; `locate` returns the root for a position outside the tree, which is not a nearest-neighbor result.

`maxDepth` defaults to 8 and `particlesPerLeaf` to 4. Deeper trees reduce cell size but increase node construction and neighbor bookkeeping. Increasing leaf capacity limits subdivision in dense populations. `timeQuality` defaults to 1; values below 1 skip some rebuilds after the first build. Check the boolean return from `rebuild` before assuming aggregates describe the current frame.

`particlesInRadius` prunes nodes using sphere-AABB intersection before exact distance tests in
leaf nodes. It is typically `O(log n + k)` for a balanced tree and `k` results, with an `O(n)`
worst case for broad queries or degenerate distributions. Options can exclude one particle index
and require matching tags. Queries use the population and node placement from the last successful
rebuild, so throttled trees may omit particles that have since crossed into the query volume.

`getNodes()` returns a new array of node references. Nodes expose bounds, neighbors, aggregate, and indices into the particle array passed to the last successful rebuild. Rebuilds replace node identities; do not retain nodes across rebuilds. Treat skipped rebuild data as stale if particles have been removed or reordered. `quantizeBounds` can stabilize moving bounds to reduce spatial churn, at the cost of looser bounds.

The [Boids example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/boids.html) demonstrates aggregation in a complete effect. Profile construction as well as query costs before increasing depth or rebuild frequency.

## GPU: ParticleSpatialGrid

Modules normally request a managed grid instead of constructing one. Set `useSpatialGrid: true`
for defaults or pass construction options through `spatialGridOptions`; the module's `modifyGPU` callback receives the
grid as its final argument. The equivalent CPU callback receives its managed octree when
`useOctree` or `octreeOptions` is configured. Boids uses this managed lifecycle with its own
aggregate format and includes particle-affector source tags in the tree population;
its GPU grid uses the same managed acquisition and cleanup as other modules.

```ts
const neighbors = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, system, octree) => {
    const neighbors = octree.particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2);
    // Compare CPU neighbors; skip particle itself when needed.
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    useSpatialGrid: true,
    spatialGridOptions: { brickSubdivisions: 3, cellSubdivisions: 4 },
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime, context, grid) => {
      grid?.forEachParticleInRadius(
        particle.position,
        float(2),
        (neighbor, distanceSquared) => {
          // Build TSL operations using neighbor and distanceSquared.
        },
        { excludeIndex: particle.index },
      );
    },
  },
);
```

Custom infrastructure can instantiate `ParticleSpatialGrid` directly, call `rebuild` with a
WebGPU renderer and `GPUParticleBufferState`, then dispose it explicitly. A positive
`maxQuerySteps` truncates traversal; zero is unbounded. Automatic bounds expansion prevents lost
particles, but because the number of cells is fixed, expanding bounds increases cell size and
reduces spatial resolution. Keep bounds tight enough for the expected population and use
`readDiagnostics` only for validation or profiling because it performs asynchronous GPU readback.
